driftTitle: Members whose published value disagrees with what this service would publish.
intro: One process, several authorization servers. The path component the two discovery shapes already carry now selects a CONFIGURATION as well as an issuer identifier — RFC 8414 section 3.1 inserts it after the well-known segment and OpenID Connect Discovery section 4 appends the well-known segment to it, which is the commonest reason a discovery fetch 404s, and this service has answered both for a long time. A path nobody has configured publishes the document this service always published, so nothing that worked before this page existed behaves differently.
noneNamed: No authorization server has been named. Every discovery URL answers with the document this service builds for itself, which is what RFC 9700 section 2.6 asks for — these are for when you need it to say something else.
label: Label
idRule: The id is a single URL path segment — letters, digits, dot, dash, underscore or tilde — because it has to appear in a URL without being escaped. One that had to be escaped would be one nobody could find again.
caveatDoes: What a document says is what that authorization server DOES. Advertise code_challenge_methods_supported: ["S256"] here and this server's own authorization endpoint refuses plain — at {path}, and nowhere else. The members marked enforced below drive behaviour; the rest are published and cannot be made true by this service, which is still useful (a document a client did not expect is a client error path worth running) and is listed as drift so that nobody discovers it the hard way.
caveatEqual: Every authorization server starts equal. A new one — or one created by somebody simply asking for it — has exactly the capabilities the default server has, and differs only where it has been made to. Every client may use every one of them: nothing here restricts a client to a server, and
caveatEqualEnd: records which ones each client has actually used. What does NOT cross between them is a credential — an authorization code issued by one is refused at another's token endpoint.
unknownMember: Not a member this service recognises — which is allowed, and is half the point: publishing something a client did not expect is what this page is for.
notPublished: Not published at all. A client reading this document cannot tell that this server supports it — which is not the same as learning that it does not, and is the difference RFC 9700 section 2.6 is arguing about.
driftWarn: {n} member(s) of this document do not describe this service. That is allowed and is often the point — but a client configured from this document will behave as though these were true.
allAgree: Every member of this document agrees with what this service would publish. A client configured from it is configured correctly.
doesNote: Its effective capabilities — the defaults every authorization server here starts with, plus whatever this one has been given. This IS the document it publishes and it IS what its endpoints enforce; there is no second table that could disagree with it.
notPublishedCheck: not published — the check does not run
noneOverridden: Nothing is overridden, so this document says exactly what this service says about itself.
publishNote: The value is read as JSON first and as a plain string if that fails, so ["S256"] is a list, false is a boolean and https://example.com/token is a string. Any member name is accepted — the list below is help rather than a schema, and one this service has never heard of is published just the same.
neverHeard: a name this service has never heard of
removeNote: Different from resetting it: reset undoes an override, this publishes an ABSENCE.
deleteNote: The two URLs go on answering — with this service's own document — because an unconfigured path has always been served that way.
